title: A compact ultracold strontium experiment
authors: Mathieu Bertrand, Torben Pöpplau, Lucas Béguin, Romain Long, Jakob Reichel
abstract: We describe a compact and simplified experimental setup for the production of ultracold strontium atoms. Thanks to its low-power oven and coil-free Zeeman slower design, the vacuum system has an overall length of only 40cm including oven, Zeeman slower and all-glass science cell. The oven has a power consumption of 14W at 460°C and produces a collimated flux of 3 10^10at/(s cm^2) at this temperature. The laser system employs master-slave laser architecture throughout and requires neither second-harmonic generation nor tapered amplifiers, reducing cost and complexity. The system has been in continuous use for more than a year.
summary: This paper details the engineering and experimental realization of a compact, low-power apparatus for producing ultracold strontium atoms. By simplifying the vacuum system and optimizing the atomic beam path, the authors achieved high flux and successfully cooled the atoms through sequential Blue and Red Magneto-Optical Trapping (MOT) stages. This work advances the practical feasibility of using Sr atoms for quantum applications.
main_problem: To describe a compact and simplified experimental setup for the production of ultracold strontium atoms.
main_result: The authors successfully developed a compact vacuum system with low power consumption, enabling the production of ultracold strontium atoms suitable for subsequent quantum experiments.
method: The experiment involves using a low-power oven and a coil-free Zeeman slower design to create a highly collimated atomic beam into a science cell.
model_or_system: The system is an atomic beam apparatus for Strontium (Sr), featuring an oven, Zeeman slower, and a science cell. It utilizes blue and red MOT stages for cooling, operating on the $1	ext{S}_0 - 1	ext{P}_1$ transition and subsequent red transitions.
key_observables: Maximum atom number ($N_b \approx 1.5 	imes 10^7$ for Blue MOT; $N \approx 2 	imes 10^7$ after compression), final temperatures ($T \approx 2.4 	ext{ mK}$), and recapture fractions ($\approx 65\%$ for Red MOT).
important_parameters: Oven power consumption ($\approx 13.5 	ext{ W}$), collimated flux ($3 \cdot 10^{10} 	ext{ atoms}\cdot	ext{s}^{-1}	ext{cm}^{-2}$), and MOT coil currents/gradients.
main_assumptions: The initial capillary angle is normal to the base surface, which is noted to reduce the atom flux compared to the desired $7^\circ$ angle.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the global and sectional views of the compact vacuum system (Fig. 1), temperature distributions (Fig. 3(a)), and optimization curves for atom number and recapture fraction versus experimental parameters (Figs. 8, 9, 10).
paper_structure: The paper details the design improvements leading to a compact apparatus, characterizes the atomic beam properties, and then describes the sequential cooling stages: Blue MOT loading, compression, and Red MOT loading, culminating in final temperature measurements.
why_interesting: The focus on engineering simplicity and reliability in an atomic source is crucial for realizing complex quantum simulations, as robust sources are often the limiting factor in quantum technology demonstrations.

FIG. 2. (a) CAD view of the oven. (b) In-situ view of the oven assembly in the sustaining flange. (Thermocouple not shown.) Low thermal conduction between the oven and the the flange is ensured by the reduced thickness of the holding plate and the nonmetallic screw sleeves and spacers.

FIG. 3. (a) Finite-element simulation of the temperature dis- tribution of the oven assembly with a heating power of 15 W. (b) Electrical power consumption vs measured oven tempera- ture (circles). The solid line is the result of the simple model described in the text; dot-dashed lines indicate its individ- ual contributions as indicated in the legend. This calculation confirms that thermal radiation is the leading contribution in the relevant temperature range.

FIG. 4. Glass cell glued to titanium flange. The cell is a low- cost catalog part intended for spectroscopy applications. The custom machined titanium flange has a coefficient of thermal expansion matching that of the glass, enabling bakeout with limited mechanical stress at the interface. The cell-flange joint is a low-outgassing epoxy glue.
